name: Amira Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does an ordinary site day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and fit timber balconies, steps and handrails on building sites. My trade certificate taught me the basics; I am a solid middle-of-the-crew carpenter who checks the fixings twice. I use AI every day to compare the cutting list with the drawing, then measure the actual slab. My partner and I have grown children, more than six months of expenses saved and a good wage; we hope I can leave regular site work at sixty-five in 2033 if our income covers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the digital cut list saves time, but someone must still test the handrail. An AI drawing cannot catch a loose balcony rail with a person leaning on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the fitting wage to last and our savings to stay strong. There are plenty of nearby building jobs, so a small change in office work does not force me to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting balconies and use the AI comparison I already know. I would check each rail fixing by hand and review our hoped-for age-sixty-five income against household costs with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work. The retirement review is due anyway; it is information, not notice that I am leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you test a rail before sign-off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check the anchors against the site specification and put weight on the finished rail where it is allowed. A tidy drawing is only one part of that check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this small scenario make you learn a new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I already use the comparison every day; I would not call my usual morning check a new AI skill.

say: I would **keep** using AI lists while physically checking balcony rails.
I would **tell** the crew that sign-off needs a real fixing check.
think: My **good** wage, long savings runway and nearby jobs make this stable.
**Checking** retirement figures is separate from deciding to retire.
do: **Keep** fitting balconies and physically checking rail anchors.
**Review** expected age-sixty-five household income against housing, food and repair costs with my partner.
feel: **Calm** about secure site work and familiar AI use.
S0.quote: An AI drawing cannot catch a loose balcony rail with a person leaning on it.
fieldNote: **Amira** uses AI daily for lists but verifies physical balcony safety by hand.
Her **higher** pay, substantial savings and many nearby builders support calm; retirement remains a budget question.

steps.text: Keep fitting and checking building-site balcony rails
Check age-sixty-five retirement budget before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faster AI balcony delivery is useless if the builder removes the paid hour for checking the rail. I would learn the new AI delivery controls early and show the crew what the records actually say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see a shorter schedule cutting my overtime or paid checking time. The household could absorb a loss, but I would not accept a safe-looking handrail signed off without the paid physical check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practice the new controls on a completed balcony order and compare two live deliveries with the site log. I would keep fitting shifts and ask for written paid inspection hours; if cuts persist, I would apply only to posted local rail-fitting roles at household-covering wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real hours risk, though our savings and the nearby jobs give me choices. I am curious about the tool and firm about the inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the new delivery control worth keeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would flag the missing anchor before the crew reaches the slab. I would check that result against two actual deliveries, not an office demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you speak to if inspection hours vanish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The site manager first, with the log and payslip. If the builder keeps cutting time, I would look at posted local jobs with adequate pay and written safety hours.

say: I would **learn** new AI delivery controls and test them against balcony orders.
I would **demand** paid time for physical handrail inspection.
think: My **overtime** or checking hours could shrink even though savings are strong.
A **useful** tool does not excuse a missing safety check.
do: **Practice** new AI delivery controls on completed and live balcony orders.
**Keep** paid fitting shifts while seeking written rail inspection hours.
**Apply** after sustained cuts to posted local rail role with adequate pay and safety time.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible paid-hour loss, with local options.
S1.quote: A faster AI balcony delivery is useless if the builder removes the paid hour for checking the rail.
fieldNote: She **learns** a genuinely new control and tests it on actual deliveries.
**Potential** loss of her paid inspection hours makes anxiety appropriate despite a strong cushion.

steps.text: Learn new AI delivery controls on real balcony orders
Keep paid rail fitting while checking written safety time
Apply after cuts to posted local rail job at adequate wage and safety time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI can plan balconies in 2028 when I am sixty, but hands-on robots arrive around 2031 when I am sixty-three. A robot fitting standard rails could cut two years of paid work before my hoped-for retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hours could shrink then, although our savings and the many nearby builders give me room to move. I would still need a safe paid role or verified retirement income to cover the years after sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a paid supervised trial checking robot-fitted rail anchors, with authority to stop unsafe handover. If paid shifts fall after 2031, I would apply to posted nearby repair or inspection roles only where wages cover the household and safety authority is written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about possible lost hours but able to act. I would not retire at sixty-three just because I have savings in an account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you refuse to sign during the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot could bolt a balcony rail in 2031, but my name should not sign a hidden anchor. I would stop handover until the rail could be checked against the site specification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the family live on the savings for two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a short spell, but we have not proved it covers life after that. We would need expected income and ongoing bills on paper before any early exit.

say: **Thinking** AI changes plans in 2028; robots may fit rails around 2031.
I would **seek** a paid supervised trial with human safety sign-off.
think: **Possible** lost fitting hours arrive two years before my target.
**Strong** savings are a bridge, not proof of an affordable early retirement.
do: **Request** paid supervised robot-rail trial with stop-handover authority.
**Keep** paid balcony shifts while trial is assessed.
**Apply** after hour cuts to posted local repair role with adequate pay and safety authority.
feel: **Anxious** about possible own-hour loss, with savings and local work.
S2.quote: A robot could bolt a balcony rail in 2031, but my name should not sign a hidden anchor.
fieldNote: Her **trial** has a specific hidden-anchor safety test and paid time.
She does **not** count savings as retirement income; any job move requires a real local adequate opening with safety authority.

steps.text: Keep paid balcony shifts while requesting a supervised paid robot trial
Apply after cuts to posted local repair job with adequate wage and safety authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am sixty-three, and capable site robots around 2034 when I am sixty-six. If our original age-sixty-five retirement in 2033 works financially, the physical robots arrive after I leave regular site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still consider formal rail inspection if the retirement budget does not work. A rail inspection certificate without the power to reject a loose fixing is just paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid balcony fitting and check our age-sixty-five income with my partner. If it falls short and a local inspector role is posted at household-covering pay with safety authority, I would complete its fully funded paid-time course and apply after qualifying; otherwise I would retire at the original target only if income covers us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until our income figures are checked. The extra time gives me a real choice between a safe paid role and the retirement we already planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the formal course add to your existing checks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The written inspection procedure and responsibility for accepting another crew’s rails. I already check my own anchors, but that is not the same authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the course yourself if the job is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It has to be fully funded and on paid days, with a posted local role at enough pay; otherwise I stay on the paid crew while we check the budget.

say: The 2034 **robot** date follows my original 2033 exit if affordable.
I would **train** for formal rail inspection only if work continues and funded paid terms exist.
think: A **checker** needs written safety authority, not merely a certificate.
The **posted** local job must pay our household bills.
do: **Enroll** if still working in funded paid-time rail course for posted adequate local safety role.
**Apply** after qualifying to posted local rail inspector job with adequate pay and safety authority.
feel: **Uneasy** until retirement income and later job terms are known.
S3.quote: A rail inspection certificate without the power to reject a loose fixing is just paper.
fieldNote: She **keeps** 2034 employment conditional on whether the original 2033 retirement target is affordable.
**Course** funding, paid days, a posted local vacancy, adequate wage and written safety authority govern training and application.

steps.text: Enroll if working in funded paid-time course for posted adequate local safety role
Apply after qualifying to posted local inspector role with adequate pay and safety authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am sixty-eight, and robots fit rails around 2039 when I am seventy-one. A rail robot in 2039 cannot replace a wage my household stopped needing in 2033, if our sums hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not assume I am still on a building site at seventy-one. If the budget fails, I may continue in paid fitting or inspection for a while, but that needs an actual nearby vacancy and safe duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep current paid balcony shifts and review age-sixty-five income and costs. If the figures cover us, I would retire at the original 2033 target; if not, I would keep working and apply only to posted local rail roles with household-covering wages and written safety authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until the budget is checked, but calm about the distant machines if it works. Ten years gives younger fitters time to learn safe checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still practise AI after retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might use it for ordinary household planning, but I am not promising to work in 2039. Our income calculation comes before any such claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep you on site after sixty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shortfall in verified income and a posted nearby job paying our bills with safe rail inspection duties. I would not work merely to prove I can use AI.

say: The 2036 and 2039 **changes** may follow my original retirement target.
I would **continue** paid site work only if the household income falls short.
think: A **distant** robot forecast does not prove I will work at seventy-one.
**Any** later role needs a real local opening, adequate wage and safe duties.
do: **Keep** current paid balcony fitting while verifying retirement income.
**Retire** at original 2033 target only if income covers ongoing household bills.
**Apply** if still working to posted local rail job with adequate pay and safety authority.
feel: **Uneasy** until retirement budget is verified, otherwise calm about distant robots.
S4.quote: A rail robot in 2039 cannot replace a wage my household stopped needing in 2033, if our sums hold.
fieldNote: Her **original** age-sixty-five exit is conditional and is not a machine-driven early retirement.
**Continued** work after 2033 requires an income shortfall plus a posted local role with adequate pay and safe authority.

steps.text: Keep paid balcony work while checking retirement budget
Retire at original 2033 target only if income covers bills
Apply if working to posted local rail role with adequate wage and safety authority

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast case worries me most because robots could cut balcony-fitting hours two years before my planned exit. A paid safety trial and a posted nearby inspector job with adequate wages and authority would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who may stop handover if a robot has hidden a loose anchor. I can learn new controls quickly, but I will not sign a rail I cannot check. A quick AI cut list cannot take the weight of a person leaning on a balcony rail.

headlineQuote: A quick AI cut list cannot take the weight of a person leaning on a balcony rail.
portrait: **Amira** is a fifty-eight-year-old trade-certified balcony carpenter with a partner and grown children.
Her **higher** wage, savings beyond six months and plentiful nearby jobs give her choices.
She **uses** AI daily and learns new controls early, while demanding physical rail safety checks.
She **hopes** to retire at sixty-five in 2033 if income permits; later site work depends on a budget shortfall.
biggestWorry: **Fast** robots around 2031 could cut paid balcony work two years before her hoped-for age-sixty-five exit.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid** supervised rail trial and a posted local inspector job with adequate wages and safety authority would help.
